header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, BAHAWALPUR BENCH,
Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties or counsel,
17.11.2026 Malik Muhammad Altaf Nawaz, Advocate for the
Mr. Jamshaid Iqbal Khakwani, learned A.A.G.
body: alongwith Muhammad Rehman, Senior Law Officer, HED, Amir Rasheed, Law Officer, HED, Rao Zahid Mehmood, Office of Director, BWP, HED and Rana Sharafat, Director, Bahawalpur, HED.

Through the instant constitutional petition, the petitioners have called in question the legality of the CTI Policy Notification bearing No. SO(EM-I)17-20/2026(CTI), dated 21.10.2026, issued by the Higher Education Department, Government of the Punjab, whereby certain amendments have been introduced in the eligibility and merit criteria for recruitment of College Teaching Interns (CTIs) for the academic session 2026-27. The principal grievance of the petitioners is directed against the introduction of a maximum age limit of 40 years, withdrawal of additional marks previously allocated to Board and University position holders, alteration of the mechanism for determining equivalence between annual and semester systems of education, and the criteria governing allocation of vacancies in male and female colleges. The petitioners seek a declaration that the impugned provisions are unconstitutional, discriminatory and without lawful authority, besides seeking restoration of the criteria contained in the previous policy.

W.P. No.6570 of 26 2 2. Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that the impugned policy has substantially altered the recruitment criteria to the disadvantage of a considerable number of qualified candidates. It is argued that the previous policy did not prescribe any upper age limit and also provided additional marks to candidates who had secured positions in their respective Boards and Universities. The newly introduced age restriction and withdrawal of such additional marks, according to learned counsel, have deprived experienced and academically distinguished candidates of an opportunity to compete for public employment. It is further contended that the previous mechanism for determining equivalence between annual and semester systems was more equitable, whereas its replacement by a uniform percentage-based formula places candidates belonging to different educational systems at an unjustified disadvantage. Learned counsel has also questioned the gender-based allocation of vacancies, contending that female candidates are permitted to compete for vacancies in boys’ BS colleges, whereas male candidates are excluded from competing for vacancies in female BS colleges. It is, thus, maintained that the impugned policy is arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution.

3. Conversely, learned Law Officer, assisted by learned Legal Advisor appearing on behalf of the respondents, has opposed the petition and contended that formulation and modification of recruitment criteria fall within the domain of the competent Government authorities. It is submitted that the impugned notification represents a policy decision taken after considering the administrative requirements of the department and the need to introduce a uniform and transparent mechanism for selection of candidates. Regarding the abolition of additional marks for position holders, it is explained that candidates emerge from different Boards and W.P. No.6570 of 26 3 Universities operating under different examination and assessment mechanisms, which had resulted in disparities and grievances in the process of merit determination. The revised criteria have, therefore, been introduced to provide uniformity in the assessment of candidates. Learned Law Officer further submits that the petitioners had an adequate remedy available before the Grievance Redressal Cell (GRC), specifically established to examine grievances arising out of the recruitment process and the applicable policy. Admittedly, the petitioners have not availed such remedy. On this ground alone, according to learned Law Officer, the instant petition is not maintainable.
4. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and have examined the available record with their able assistance.

5. Before adverting to the individual grounds of challenge, it would be appropriate to examine the scope of constitutional jurisdiction in matters relating to formulation and alteration of recruitment policies by the competent Government authorities. It is an established principle that policy-making primarily falls within the domain of the Federal or Provincial Government, as the case may be. The Government, being the employer, is competent to determine the qualifications, eligibility conditions, age limits, method of assessment and other relevant criteria considered necessary for recruitment against posts within its administrative domain. Such criteria may be modified or replaced in the light of changing administrative requirements, institutional needs and considerations of uniformity and transparency. The fact that a particular criterion existed under an earlier policy does not, by itself, create an indefeasible right in prospective candidates to insist that the same criterion must continue to govern every subsequent recruitment exercise.

6. The above principle finds support from the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Watan Party and W.P. No.6570 of 26 4 another v. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2013 Supreme Court 167), wherein it has been held that formulation of policy is essentially within the domain of the Federal or Provincial Government and that Courts ordinarily do not interfere in policy matters unless the impugned action is shown to be mala fide or violative of the fundamental rights of citizens. It has further been observed that Courts cannot sit in judgment over policy decisions of the competent authorities where such decisions have been taken after due consideration and deliberation. The underlying rationale is that the wisdom, suitability and administrative desirability of a policy are matters primarily entrusted to the executive, whereas the function of the Court is confined to examining its legality and constitutional validity. Thus, the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court cannot be invoked merely to substitute one permissible policy choice with another on the ground that the latter may be more beneficial or advantageous to a particular category of persons.

7. Needless to observe that the power of the executive to formulate policy is not absolute or beyond judicial scrutiny. A policy decision may undoubtedly be examined by this Court where it is shown to have been made in violation of the Constitution or law, to suffer from patent arbitrariness, to be founded upon mala fide considerations, or to result in an unreasonable and discriminatory classification. However, the exercise of constitutional jurisdiction does not extend to substituting the Court’s own assessment of administrative suitability for that of the competent authority merely because another policy choice may also appear reasonable or preferable. The distinction between judicial review of the legality of a policy and judicial evaluation of its administrative wisdom must, therefore, be maintained.

8. The question of mala fide, in particular, requires more than a general allegation or an expression of dissatisfaction W.P. No.6570 of 26 5 with the outcome of an administrative decision. It is essentially a question of fact which must be specifically pleaded and established through cogent material. In this regard, guidance may be sought from the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Dr. Akhtar Hassan Khan and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2012 SCMR 455), wherein the principle has been recognised that, in the absence of specifically pleaded and established mala fide, a policy framed by the competent authority, backed by law and not shown to suffer from illegality or arbitrariness, is ordinarily not open to interference in judicial review. Thus, a mere assertion that the revised criteria are disadvantageous to certain candidates, or that the previous policy was comparatively more favourable, cannot be treated as sufficient proof of mala fide or arbitrary exercise of authority. The person alleging mala fide bears the burden of establishing the same through specific pleadings and supporting material, which burden cannot be discharged through mere conjectures, apprehensions or assumptions.

9. In the present case, the petitioners have principally relied upon the comparison between the recruitment criteria contained in the previous policy and those introduced through the impugned notification. Their grievance, in substance, is that certain benefits previously available to prospective candidates have been withdrawn. However, the mere fact that the Government has altered the age limit, the allocation of marks or the mechanism for assessing academic merit does not, in itself, establish that the revised criteria are unconstitutional. The petitioners were required to demonstrate that the amendments suffer from some identifiable legal infirmity, such as absence of lawful authority, manifest arbitrariness, hostile discrimination or mala fide exercise of power. A general assertion that the previous criteria were W.P. No.6570 of 26 6 more beneficial or equitable cannot, by itself, furnish sufficient ground for invalidating the subsequent policy.

10. So far as the introduction of a maximum age limit of 40 years is concerned, prescription of an age ceiling for recruitment is ordinarily a matter falling within the competence of the employer, subject, of course, to the applicable law and constitutional limitations. The petitioners have not been able to demonstrate from the material placed on record that the prescribed age limit is contrary to any statutory provision or that the competent authority lacked the power to introduce such restriction. Nor has any specific material been brought to the notice of this Court establishing that the age restriction has been introduced with an ulterior motive to exclude the petitioners or any particular class of candidates. The circumstance that the previous policy did not prescribe an upper age limit does not, by itself, render the subsequently prescribed age ceiling unlawful. A candidate who was eligible under an earlier recruitment policy does not acquire a vested right to claim continuation of the same eligibility conditions in a subsequent recruitment exercise.

11. The objection relating to withdrawal of additional marks for Board and University position holders also does not persuade this Court to interfere. Awarding additional marks for academic distinctions is one of the possible methods of assessing merit; however, it is not the only constitutionally permissible method. The competent authority may adopt a different mechanism for evaluating candidates, provided that the same is applied uniformly and does not offend any provision of law. The explanation furnished by the respondents that the earlier arrangement had generated disparities and grievances because of different examination and assessment systems prevailing in various educational institutions cannot be brushed aside as wholly irrelevant. The Government has opted for a revised mechanism with the W.P. No.6570 of 26 7 stated object of achieving uniformity in merit determination. Whether the earlier system was comparatively more advantageous to certain candidates is not the test for determining the legality of the new arrangement. In the absence of material demonstrating that the revised mechanism is inherently arbitrary or has been devised to favour or exclude a particular individual or class without lawful justification, this Court would not be justified in restoring the previous arrangement merely on the basis of comparative preference.

12. The argument concerning equivalence between the annual and semester systems of education is also to be examined in the same perspective. Different educational systems may adopt different methods of assessment, grading and declaration of results. It is primarily for the competent authority to devise an appropriate mechanism for comparing the academic performance of candidates emerging from such systems. The petitioners may have a legitimate grievance regarding the comparative impact of the revised formula; nevertheless, the existence of a different or more favourable formula under the previous policy does not establish that the new mechanism is necessarily unlawful. No concrete comparative data, technical assessment or other material has been placed before this Court to establish that the revised method produces an irrational distinction or systematically disadvantages a particular category of candidates in a manner prohibited by the Constitution. In the absence of such material, the Court would be reluctant to undertake an exercise of substituting its own academic assessment mechanism for the one adopted by the competent department.

13. As regards the objection relating to gender-based allocation of vacancies in male and female BS colleges, the petitioners have relied upon Articles 25 and 27 of the Constitution. There can be no cavil with the proposition that W.P. No.6570 of 26 8 public employment must be governed by fairness, equality and non-discrimination. At the same time, every distinction in the allocation of institutional vacancies does not necessarily constitute prohibited discrimination. The nature of the institution, its institutional character and the requirements of the teaching environment may be relevant considerations in determining the suitability and allocation of teaching positions. Article 25(3) of the Constitution also recognises the competence of the State to make special provisions for the protection of women and children. Therefore, the mere fact that different eligibility arrangements have been prescribed for vacancies in male and female colleges would not, without examining their object, rationale and practical operation, be sufficient to declare the policy unconstitutional. The petitioners have not placed any material before this Court to establish that the impugned arrangement is founded upon an impermissible consideration or that it operates in a manner which amounts to an unjustified exclusion from public employment. Accordingly, no case for constitutional interference on this ground is made out.

14. It is also significant that the petitioners have invoked Articles 37(b) and 38(e) of the Constitution in support of their challenge. But the learned counsel for the petitioners has not explained how these Articles are attracted to the present case. These provisions form part of the Principles of Policy contained in Part II, Chapter 2 of the Constitution. Their application, however, is subject to Article 30(2) of the Constitution, which expressly provides that the validity of a law or action cannot be questioned merely on the ground that it is inconsistent with the Principles of Policy. Consequently, these provisions, in the circumstances of the present case, cannot independently furnish a basis for striking down the impugned recruitment policy in the absence of an established violation of an enforceable constitutional or statutory right. W.P. No.6570 of 26 9 15. Another significant aspect of the matter is the availability of an alternative remedy before the Grievance Redressal Cell (GRC). Learned Law Officer has categorically stated that the said forum is available to examine grievances arising out of the recruitment policy and the selection process. The petitioners have not disputed the availability of such remedy, nor have they shown that any representation or grievance was submitted before the said forum or that the same was declined to be entertained. The principle governing exercise of constitutional jurisdiction is well settled: where an adequate and efficacious alternative remedy is available, this Court ordinarily refrains from exercising its extraordinary jurisdiction, particularly when the controversy requires examination of matters falling within the administrative and technical domain of the competent department. Although the existence of an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar to the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution, a petitioner seeking to bypass such remedy must demonstrate circumstances justifying direct intervention by this Court, such as patent want of jurisdiction, violation of an express statutory provision or an apparent infringement of fundamental rights warranting immediate constitutional protection. No such exceptional circumstance has been established in the present case. The petitioners, having approached this Court without first availing the available grievance redressal mechanism, have not furnished any convincing justification for bypassing the forum specifically available to address their grievances. This omission assumes particular significance when the controversy involves the comparative operation of recruitment criteria and the administrative rationale underlying their modification.

16. It is equally important to appreciate that the impugned notification governs a recruitment exercise involving a substantial number of vacancies and a large pool of W.P. No.6570 of 26 10 prospective candidates. The relief sought by the petitioners, particularly restoration of the previous policy framework and suspension of the revised criteria, would have consequences extending far beyond their individual claims and would directly affect other candidates who may be participating in the recruitment process under the newly notified criteria. Any interference with an ongoing recruitment exercise must, therefore, be founded upon a clear and demonstrable legal infirmity rather than upon a general apprehension that the revised policy may be less advantageous to certain categories of applicants. The Court must remain mindful that the process of recruitment involves competing interests of numerous candidates, and an intervention unsupported by a legally sustainable basis may itself create uncertainty and prejudice in the selection process.

17. Perusal of the record further reveals that the petitioners have challenged the policy principally on the basis of its comparison with the preceding recruitment framework. However, they have not been able to establish that any accrued right has been taken away, that the impugned amendments have been applied retrospectively to a completed selection process, or that the competent authority has acted beyond the powers vested in it. No specific instance of mala fide, favouritism or deliberate manipulation of the revised criteria has been substantiated. In view of the principles enunciated in Watan Party (supra) and Dr. Akhtar Hassan Khan (supra), the absence of specific pleadings and supporting material establishing mala fide or patent illegality assumes considerable significance. The mere assertion that the previous policy offered better opportunities to academically distinguished or relatively older candidates cannot be elevated to the level of a constitutional violation. A recruitment policy is required to be assessed on the touchstone of legality, reasonableness and constitutional compliance, and not merely W.P. No.6570 of 26 11 by comparing the advantages available under successive administrative arrangements.

18. The scope of judicial review of policy decisions and the constitutional balance between the executive and judiciary have been elaborately discussed in a plethora of judgments. It is well settled that formulation and modification of policy primarily fall within the domain of the competent executive authority, and the Courts ordinarily do not examine its wisdom, suitability or adequacy. Judicial interference is warranted only where a policy is shown to be contrary to the Constitution or law, violative of fundamental rights, mala fide, arbitrary or discriminatory, or otherwise beyond lawful authority. The Courts must, therefore, exercise judicial restraint and respect the constitutional boundaries of different organs of the State, as unwarranted interference would offend the principle of separation of powers. Reliance in this regard may be placed upon Lahore Development Authority through D.G. and others vs. M/s.Imrana Tiwana and others (2015 SCMR 1739), Mubarak Ali Babar vs. Punjab Public Service Commission through its Secretary and others (2023 SCMR 518), Syed Hammad Nabi and others vs. Inspector General of Police Punjab, Lahore and others (2023 SCMR 584), Vice Chancellor Agricultural University, Peshawar and others vs. Muhammad Shafiq and others (2024 SCMR 527), Senior General Manager, Pakistan Railways and others vs.Muhammad Pervaiz (2024 SCMR 581) and Naseem Khan and others vs. Government of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Chief Secretary Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Peshawar and others (2024 SCMR 1341) In the present case, no such exceptional circumstance has been established warranting interference by this Court.

19. In the circumstances, this Court is of the considered view that the petitioners have failed to establish any patent W.P. No.6570 of 26 12 illegality, jurisdictional defect, mala fide or demonstrable constitutional infirmity in the impugned notification warranting interference under Article 199 of the Constitution. The policy decision in question falls within the administrative domain of the competent Government authority, and no material has been brought on record to demonstrate that the same suffers from any such legal infirmity as would justify judicial interference. The availability of an alternative grievance redressal mechanism, which has admittedly not been availed, provides an additional reason for declining to exercise extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction in the matter. Needless to observe that the respondents remain under an obligation to administer the impugned policy fairly, uniformly and strictly in accordance with law, and any individual grievance arising from its implementation may be agitated before the competent forum in accordance with law.
20. For what has been discussed above, the instant constitutional petition, being devoid of merit.
C. M. No. 4598 of 2026 21. As the main writ petition has been dismissed, hence, this application stands disposed of having become infructuous.
(Syed Ahsan Raza Kazmi)
Judge Approved for reporting.
